paras: The disappearance of Mormon elders Davis and Weaver occurred in Clay County, Alabama, in August 1888, when two missionaries vanished a day after a body of masked men ordered them to leave the county. A Birmingham dispatch reported that they were "generally believed" to have been murdered by local citizens and their bodies concealed, and a later item credited to the Clay County Leader said flatly that they had been killed. No report of their bodies being found appears in the coverage.

According to the Birmingham dispatch, Mormon missionaries had worked in Clay County for about four years and made many converts, most of them women who were "hurried off to Utah." Hostility grew after a convert wrote to relatives from Salt Lake City describing polygamy and "outrages" against Alabama converts, and the elders were ordered to leave but refused. The dispatch said feeling among "the better class of citizens" reached "fever heat" on the Sunday before August 23, when Davis and Weaver were said to have immersed converts of both sexes in a mill pond "in a perfectly nude condition" before about fifty people.

Many threats against the elders followed the baptism. On Monday night a body of masked men went to the house where the two were boarding and ordered them to leave the county within twenty-four hours. The elders reportedly defied the crowd and the next morning set out alone for the neighborhood of Lineville to hold services at a convert's house, after which they were not seen or heard of again.

No report of a search, an inquest, arrests or a trial appears in the coverage. A month later the Iuka Reporter in Mississippi ran a one-line item credited to the Clay County Leader stating that the two elders "were killed" for the nude baptism, without new details.

The Atlanta Constitution printed the Birmingham special on August 28 under the headline "Have They Been Murdered?" and framed the case as a "mysterious disappearance." Its account dwelt on polygamy, the women converts sent to Utah and the nude baptism, and it described the presumed killers only as "the indignant citizens of the county." The same text ran as a wire story in the Maysville Evening Bulletin under "Two Mormon Elders" and in the Hillsboro, Ohio, News-Herald under "Missing Mormons," with datelines varying from August 23 to August 27.

Shorter notices hardened the language. The Savannah Courier in Tennessee said the elders had been "boldly proselyting" and were believed "lynched," while the Iuka Reporter's later item treated their deaths as settled. The Salt Lake Herald reprinted the Constitution's special in full on September 6, credited to the Atlanta paper. None of the reports gave the elders' first names or race.

The August wire reports called the elders' fate a "supposed murder," resting on general belief, whereas the September item credited to the Clay County Leader stated that they "were killed." The later item offered no body, witness or other evidence beyond the details already in the wire.

bases: A body of masked men ordered two Mormon elders out of the county, after which they vanished and were 'generally believed' murdered by local citizens, and a later brief says they 'were killed' (A2, A11).

A body of masked men warned the elders to leave, and the papers reported it was 'generally believed' they had been murdered by 'indignant citizens', with a later Clay County Leader item saying they were killed for a nude baptism (A2, A1, A11); no body, inquest or other confirmation of death was reported, so the killing rests on belief and one flat statement.

The detailed account comes from one Birmingham dispatch reprinted widely (A1, A2, A4, A10); the Clay County Leader item (A11) agrees that the elders were killed but repeats the wire's details, so its independence cannot be established, and no report confirms the deaths.
